source.title: Exploring Training and Inference Scaling Laws in Generative Retrieval
source.authors: Hong-Ru Cai; Yong-Qi Li; Rui-Feng Yuan; Wen-Jie Wang; Zhen Zhang; Wen-Jie Li; Tat-Seng Chua

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some plotted point values are not provided in the text, but the authors describe the trends and report fitted parameters.
record.tranche_reason: The study investigates scaling in generative retrieval, a new task setting, using fine-tuned models and retrieval-performance measures rather than held-out language-model pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own retrieval-performance scaling results, which bear on V6 and on setup dependence in V7. It does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy, validate predictions from small runs on much larger runs, find a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, or test architecture shape at fixed parameter count. The CGL-versus-ranking-metrics validation is not a scaling result and is not recorded as a row.
record.test_reason: The study fits power laws to held-out test loss (CGL) of fine-tuned pretrained T5 and LLaMA-2 models in a new setting, generative retrieval. It varies backbone size and fine-tuning data size. This bears on V5 (power laws under fine-tuning) and V6 (downstream task performance improving with scale). The beam-size sweeps scale inference compute, an axis no version names.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also stress that LLaMA consistently outperforms T5 under identical conditions, suggesting an advantage for larger decoder-only models. They frame CGL as valid for relative comparison only, and note that the two identifier methods used different datasets.
record.recipe_differences: The study fine-tunes pretrained T5 and LLaMA models for generative retrieval and measures retrieval-specific CGL and Miss Rate, rather than measuring held-out pretraining cross-entropy across language-model pretraining runs.
record.method_sensitivity: Scaling outcomes vary by identifier method: n-gram retrieval shows model-size scaling, while codebook retrieval does not in the reported setup. Data-scaling exponents differ between n-gram and codebook methods. Inference Miss Rate trends and fitted parameters vary by model and retrieval threshold. The authors also report different low- versus high-compute comparisons between T5-Base and LLaMA-7B.

fits_no_version.finding: Miss Rate falls as a saturating power law in inference FLOPs per query, varied through beam size, for T5-Base and LLaMA-7B. T5-Base is better below about 1e11 FLOPs; LLaMA-7B is better above it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Task performance scales as a power law in inference-time compute.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval (SIGIR ’25)
record.problems: The study uses retrieval-specific CGL rather than held-out language-model pretraining loss; the authors caution that CGL does not directly guarantee traditional retrieval-metric performance. Codebook model-size scaling was tested with one epoch, which the authors say may be insufficient. The identifier methods use different datasets, limiting their direct comparison. Error bars or confidence intervals are not reported for the fitted results.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute; no pretraining runs.
Extrapolation from small runs to much larger runs; no held-out prediction.
Architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
Image, video and repeated-data regimes; anything beyond fine-tuning for retrieval.
Link between pretraining loss and downstream performance; standard benchmark tasks; predictive (extrapolated) accuracy.
Dependence of exponents on parameter counting, schedule or fitting method; disagreement between published laws.

record.verdict_notes: V7 links were dropped: different exponents across retrieval tasks are not fitting-choice dependence of pretraining laws. All fits are least-squares with no uncertainty reported. The LLaMA model-size fit uses 3 points for 3 parameters. P counts backbone non-embedding parameters, although training used LoRA. CGL is a contrastive ratio of generation losses, not cross-entropy; the authors say it does not guarantee better recall.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss as a function of parameters, training tokens, or training compute.
Whether fits from small runs predict outcomes for runs orders of magnitude larger.
The loss-minimising parameter/token split at fixed training compute and its trend with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
Power laws for held-out language-model loss across other modalities or training regimes. The paper studies retrieval performance after task fine-tuning, not pretraining loss.
The study tests scaling of generative-retrieval performance, not broad downstream-task performance or its relationship to pretraining loss.
Dependence of language-model pretraining exponents on parameter-counting conventions, fitting choices, and training schedules; published-law disagreements; and compute-optimal allocation.

rows.operation_detail: Varied model size for n-gram-based generative retrieval and fitted a power law to test-set contrastive generation loss.
rows.measure: Test-set contrastive generation loss (CGL) versus number of non-embedding parameters
rows.note: The fitted curve is reported for the T5 series as a family-level result, not as separate numeric CGL values for each T5 checkpoint.
rows.check: Re-linked from V6/V7 to V5/V6. This is fine-tuned task loss versus backbone size, five T5 points. Exponent differences across setups are task variation, not V7's fitting-choice dependence of pretraining laws.

relationships.condition: Fine-tuning for n-gram retrieval (backbone-size and data sweeps) and codebook retrieval (data sweep)
relationships.reason: Test CGL fits saturating power laws in model size (R1, R2), data size (R5, R6) and jointly (R7), with R² 0.976–0.999. LLaMA-2 has only three sizes.
relationships.display_finding: Test CGL fitted separate and joint saturating power laws in model and data size with R² of 0.976–0.999, although LLaMA-2 used only three sizes.

relationships.condition: Codebook retrieval (new vocabulary tokens, one epoch) when backbone size is varied
relationships.reason: CGL fluctuates with no consistent trend across T5 or LLaMA sizes (R3, R4). The authors attribute this to one epoch being insufficient.
relationships.display_finding: CGL fluctuated without a consistent trend across T5 and LLaMA sizes, which the authors attributed to insufficient training.

relationships.condition: n-gram generative retrieval across backbone size; both identifier methods across fine-tuning data
relationships.reason: Retrieval CGL falls smoothly with backbone size and fine-tuning data (R1, R2, R5, R6, R7).
relationships.display_finding: Retrieval CGL decreased smoothly with larger backbones for n-gram identifiers and with more fine-tuning data for both identifier methods.

relationships.condition: Codebook generative retrieval across backbone size
relationships.reason: No consistent improvement with model size (R3, R4); scale helps downstream only for some identifier methods.
relationships.display_finding: Retrieval performance showed no consistent improvement with backbone size, making scaling gains dependent on the identifier method.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Tested generative-retrieval settings: n-gram retrieval with model-size and data-size sweeps, codebook retrieval with a data-size sweep, and n-gram inference-compute sweeps
reader_labels.reason: The reported retrieval measures improve with increased model size for n-gram retrieval, increased training data for both identifier methods, and increased inference compute; see R1–R2 and R5–R13.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Codebook retrieval when model size is varied
reader_labels.reason: Neither the T5 nor LLaMA series shows a consistent CGL reduction with larger model size in the reported one-epoch setup; see R3–R4.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Identifier-method comparisons across model-size and data-size scaling
reader_labels.reason: Scaling behavior depends on the retrieval setup: n-gram model-size scaling is fitted, while codebook model-size scaling has no consistent trend, and the reported data-scaling exponents differ by identifier method; see R1–R6.
